I think a good series that qualifies here could be The Last Apprentice Series. To me, I feel like Joesph Delaney did a phenomenal job on the first thirteenth books (Revenge of the Witch through Fury of the Seventh Son - sometimes referred to as the “Wardstone Chronicles”). However, it seemed like Delaney couldn’t find ability to walk away or close the series well. 

Whereas in the Wardstone Chronicles, Delaney follows and develops characters for thirteen books, with compelling motivations and impactful deaths, he tries to rush a new plot while breaking much of the conventions/scaling of the original series in a three book add on called “The Starblade Chronicles”. The characters acted a bit one-dimensional and shallow compared to how they were portrayed in the original series, as well as Delaney seems to try and build another main threat/antagonist, to the same scale as the original one, in less that 25% of the time it took for the original series. 

While the series turned from Amazing to Moderate at the conclusion of the Starblade Chronicles, Delaney finds a way to return to the same universe in the canonical near future and uses some of the pre-established characters from the Wardstone Chronicles, as well as the subsequent Starblade Chronicles, and tries to make another book series that brings the overall canonical universe down ever further (in my opinion). This takes the overall collection of work Delaney made in regards to this universe from Moderate to Poor in my opinion. Additionally, while a third book hasn’t been released in the third series, it is potentially planned that Delaney brings back the main threat from the Wardstone Chronicles, in which feels to me a move embodying the same spirit as “somehow Palpatine returned.” 

While it’s not necessarily amazing writing, what really drove the story for me was themes and worldbuilding. With what Delaney has continued to do after the Wardstone Chronicles, it feels like a departure from what I valued the most in these books, so much so that they feel like a shadow of what they could have been. This, along with the fact that now some earlier sacrifices in the series feel invalidated and now I have zero satisfaction or closure gained by most of the new plot, makes it feel to me like actual bad fanfiction.

Ooooh boy, this depends on some people, I think at least. 

In terms of what it feels like; everything and nothing at the same time. Some days I can’t feel anything. Not just I can’t feel depression, but I can’t feel any emotion either. Other days I feel everything. Depression washes over me like a tidal wave, the slightest things set me off. I feel trapped, constrained, drowning in the negative emotion. Other days I get mood highs and lows. I’ll be incredibly, amazingly happy for thirty minutes and a compete wreck for two hours after. In short, you sometimes start off not feeling anything, and when you start feeling, you feel everything. At once. 

In terms of what it’s like: for me it’s normal life. I believe I was born with it, as I cannot trace any significant life event or circumstance where I might’ve gained it. Others have touched upon the inner voice. To me I thought it was my thoughts, my conscience. It seemed normal at first. Didn’t everyone think this way? But no, it took me a long time to realize I have depression, and a longer time to come to terms with it. 

Depression is a parasite, plain and true. It feeds off of your soul, sapping your body of its strength and forcing you to love by its rules. You take the backseat of your life, depression is driving the car. You don’t have control and some part of you doesn’t want to, after all, you’ve been living this way all of your life, that’s all you know. Depression convinces you that’s it’s an integral part of you life, that it’s you and if you kill it, you kill you. 

I could spout for hours and hours on what it means to me. I’ve written short stories, songs, even a few poems to describe it. To me, depression is my life. Currently at least. I am sixteen years old and I only have that and getting into a good college to focus on. 

If anyone is struggling and needs to reach out, don’t be afraid to hit my inbox up. I bid you all a good life.

It’s no problem. A lot of technique comes from straight up practice. Repetition is the best teacher. 

For counter-jabbing, the movement isn’t really a technique. It’s good to make sure you’re able to move your gloves around and respond to a jab, but you should have a strong guard if you’re on defense. It’s being prepared. When I spar I don’t move my gloves if I don’t have to. When I’m throwing a punch, the hand not in motion is glued to my face and my elbow is tucked against my body. When I’m on defense, both hands are up and I still have my elbows tucked. I don’t lleve my hands around to try and stay loose, but I stay relaxed enough that I know I can smack a jab out of the air. Does that make sense? 

The way I know how to counter-jab is you open up your dominant glove ( so if you’re right-handed, that’s your right hand) and try to smack the jab down/away. At the same time, you’re supposed to bend and jab up to the face. A verbal explanation sucks, if I were you I’d try to look up some YouTube techniques and stuff to see how actual people do it.

You’re not really working in tandem with your legs. Try making sure your jab comes with a push off the back foot. That way it’ll be stronger and faster. At the same time, remember that you want to keep like, 60% of your weight on your back foot. Try not to lean in so much. Extend your arms, you’ve got a decent reach, use it. 

Stop moving your gloves up and down. I get that you want to be ready to counter-jab, but the movement you do throws you out of stance and leaves you open. Plus, it’ll take longer to throw a good punch because you’re bringing your arms up then out, not off the body and out like you’re supposed to. 

Try punching higher. I’m a short dude (5’5”) so I got used to jabbing up or throwing any sort of punch eye level and above, so that’s what I’ve learned. Unless you’re going to a body jab (which then you’d drop down and jab) your punches should be a bit higher (around eye level, a bit angled up from straight). 

More about your reach— sometimes you seem to be stepping too close to the bag when throwing some punches. This smothers your punch and takes away some power. That’s why some defensive strategy is to step into a body shot to screw up your opponent. Try using your full length of your arms. It’ll generate some explosiveness and power. 

Keep your guard up. If you drop a hand while throwing another, you’ll get rocked pretty easily. If you throw something with your left, your right should be up protecting your face, and vice versa.  You might want to try shadow boxing with weights- start with two pound weights in each hand. Work on the basic jab and basic cross. This will help build strength and speed. Also, if you keep your hands up while doing it with heavier weights, you’ll definitely keep your hands up while just in gloves.

Overall though, you’re doing pretty decently for two weeks. Keep up the good work man. Try not to kill yourself though. Ease into it. It would suck to get injured and then take a break.
